One should apply a lamp in the form of the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) to each of the throat, chest, feet, and eyes.
Those who are uninitiated, those who are foolish, those who have not fallen [from their status], and those who are deficient in limbs—
the cave-temple should be established for the sake of removing defects of vision;
likewise, [the image] should be placed upon three stones at the base.
By performing many recitations (*japa*), one destroys previously accumulated merit in the event of a national upheaval,
when a king has been deposed, during illness, at the time of funeral rites,
or when the twilight worship (*sandhyā-vandana*) has been interrupted; [in these cases], there is never any fault.
And at festivals, during the hoisting of banners, and in sacrificial rites involving the erection of ritual poles.
If the twilight worship (sandhyāvandana) is interrupted, there is never any fault;
one should remain seated on a beautiful seat to the right side of the deity.
It should be performed with the root mantra, as well as with the water of the Śiva-gāyatrī;
thus there shall be the final great consecration for the Lord of Umā.
They are capable of devouring the three worlds.
Rice accompanied by fruit and coconut—
these offerings of fruit bestow [merit].
Likewise, rice, split mung beans, molasses, and *kṛsara* (rice and lentil porridge).
One should offer plantains and coconuts to Nandīśa.
O Śaṅkara, he who seeks my devotees and he who seeks my form—
both of them go to hell for as long as the moon, the sun, and the sprouts of the earth endure.
The gross liṅga is the vimāna, and the subtle liṅga is Sadāśiva;
one should worship the threefold liṅga, including the balipīṭha and the bhadra-liṅga,
in front, on the bull, to the left, nearby, or within the sanctum.
A circumambulation and prostration destroy previously accumulated merit.
[This applies] during a royal consecration, the giving away of a daughter, and the worship [of deities],
as well as at the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*) and sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), except for the month-long [observance].
One should place Vighneśa with a water-form (jalabera), Tāṇḍava, and Umāpati;
in the center, Sarvatra, Naivedya, Pārvatī, and Caṇḍavaiḍhṛva.
These two forms may be on a single pedestal, or the installation may be performed according to their distinct forms.
One should present the *ārātrika* lamp and the food offering (*naivedya*) together in a single vessel.
Having installed the image of Soma-Āskandana-Ṭeśa, who bears the moon as his crest-jewel and the sun as his eye, one should perform the rite today; one must not have [another] image fashioned.
Five darbha blades are prescribed for auspicious rites, while seven darbha blades are used for daily obligatory rites;
three darbha blades are required for ancestral rites (pitṛkārya), and one blade each for rites for the deceased (pretakārya).
Likewise, kuśa, kāśa, dūrvā, prahiba, and mauñja grasses are also employed.
The Viśvāmitras and the Yavas are proclaimed to be [the types of] Darbha grass.
One should offer bilva leaves for a year, tulasī leaves for six months,
a lotus leaf for a fortnight, and karavīra flowers for three nights.
Caṇḍa and Vṛṣa, as well as Somasūtra; Caṇḍa and Somasūtra again, then Caṇḍa and once more Vṛṣa.
[One should worship] that which resides in the Liṅga, that which resides in the Jar, that which resides in the Kuṇḍa, and likewise the Maṇḍala.
The heart of the Ācārya is the embodiment of the five forms. (P.
9a, 1st line) …one hundred people [attain] merit; one thousand [attain] the merit of anointment;
one hundred thousand garlands and an infinite lamp are said [to be attained].
At the wrist, Brahmā himself is always present; with the thumb is Sadāśiva;
Īśvara is said to be on the index finger; and Śiva is threefold in the middle finger.
Vighnarāja is on the ring finger, and Skanda is indeed on the little finger.
On the surface of the earth, the moon and sun are his nails, and the stars are his deities.
On the line, at the seven sacred sites (*saptatīrtha*): these are the characteristics of the hand. The substances for consecration (*abhiṣeka*) are as follows:
oil, which bestows happiness upon the kingdom, purifies, and destroys evil, along with products of the cow (*gavyaka*).
Bestowing glory, fame, happiness, and auspiciousness, it grants the fruit of truth and knowledge through the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and so forth; [it consists of] curd, ghee, … (P.
9b, 1st line) … suitable [substances], honey, and the pacifying [element].
The Rākṣasa, with fruits made of the essence of sugarcane and [other] desirable things, [delighted him].

The bathing with coconut water grants the happiness of kingship, while that with scented water [grants it] until the vow is completed; such is the procedure for the consecration with those jars, which bestows both desired objects and liberation.
From the divine cow, milk is produced as a single source for the mantra;
from that [milk], the tantra of manifold forms is born.
Whether for the blink of an eye or even for the duration of a moment,
one who arises devoted to the service of Śiva is honored in the world of Śiva for thousands of divine years.
One who obstructs a disciple, one who betrays Śiva,
and a sinner go to the Raurava hell for as long as the moon and sun endure.
By five, six, seven, nine, ten, and eleven [divisions], [the remainder] is the sun, the hand, the arrow, ...
(P.10a, 1st line) ... its ninth part is ten.
That altar for worship, with its single outer enclosure consisting of the stations of the vow, is [surrounded] by sacrificial pits.
O twice-born Śiva, one should perform the rite for the conception of the embryo in the center of that [area];
however, the study of the Vedas by the Brahmins should take place near the half-pavilion.
The bathing ceremony for the initiated ascetics was held in the vicinity of the bathing pavilion;
that for the women of the royal family was held in the vicinity of the great pavilion.
And for initiated Śūdras, [the dance] shall take place near the dancing pavilion;
and for uninitiated Śūdras, it shall take place near the gateway of the city gate.
Having seen the stūpa of all others as well, one pays homage;
the lamp-stand, the consecration, and the offering of water have a single fruit.
One should perform the consecration of the deity who is worshipped with variegated flowers;
likewise, one should provide the characteristics of ornaments and lamps, as well as lamps at the doors and the nine powers (*navaśakti*).
One should worship the seven mothers of the seven-lamp-maker and Unmanī, the animal of the five lamps; otherwise, there would be the fault of failing to bring about the observance.
One should worship the sun and the archway (toraṇa), as well as the guardians of the directions at the four gates and other locations;
one should also place the eight banners, the eight elephants, the eight auspicious objects (maṅgala), and water near the altar.
The pavilion for the ritual of Hastobhavya is pure; it possesses the Vāstu and Īśāna pitchers.
It is provided with the weapons-pitchers of the world-protectors, the Ardhinī pitcher, the Gaṇeśa pitcher, and the fire on the sacrificial altar.
On the northern portion of the eastern door, there are two pitchers for Nandi and Śānti.
There, in three water-pots situated to the south, one should worship Indra, Kāla, and Ravi.
One should worship a single jar in the south-eastern direction;
in the eastern direction of the south [i.e., the southeast], there are two jars for the Bhṛṅgi-vidyā.
After that, one should worship Yamavighneśa with a pair of water-jars. In the southwest, within three water-jars, one should worship Brahmā, Niṛti, and Keśava (the Corpse).
One should worship a pair of jars in the western and southern directions;
in the northwest, one should worship Vāyu, Vighneśa, and a pair of jars.

One should worship [the two pitchers] at the northern and western parts of the double-pitcher (dvikumbha). To the east of that is the installation of Gaurī, and for those two [are the deities] Soma and Caṇḍaka.
In the northeast, one should worship the Guru in three water-pots, and Īśvara in the [northeast] pot; one should worship Vidhi in the west of Indra;
and on the left, Saumya in the direction of the Vedas, at the distance of four pots.
Three pitchers each for Nirṛti, two each for Īśa and Kadrū;
one pitcher for Varuṇa in the west, and Agni for Agni and Vāyu. (L.
A mirror, a full pitcher, a bull, and a pair of chowries.
He bears the Śrīvatsa, the Svastika, the conch, the lamp, and the eight auspicious symbols;
he has five equal faces on his face, with an equal nose and eyes;
he has ten ears, ten arms, and holds ten tridents in his hands.
The neck is one and the heart is of an intensely red color;
thus is the nature of the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha), consisting of two feet.
Rudrākṣa, holding fire in his hand, accompanied by the Lord of Stars (the Moon),
his limbs smeared with ashes, exultant upon a lotus-seat, accompanied by hosts of sages, and with Gaṅgā as his companion upon his head.
Śivā [beheld] the syllable Oṃ, the root mantra, accompanied by the hosts of sages, the essence of the Vedas,
having the color of reddish rays, with hair as white as nectar, and a casket.
In her hands she holds a hand-drum (ḍamaruka), a trident, a sword, and a skull-cup; she has fire-like eyes, a serpent for a seat, and is joined with a lotus.
Śītalā Devī is the mother of the entire world, worshipped by the Siddhas.
The goddess Reṇukā is meditating; in her left [hands] she holds a trident, a skull-bowl, a rosary, and a lotus-stalk,
while she bears a garland of heads with her lotus-like hands.

One should take refuge in Śrī Renukā, who is radiant with ornaments of serpents, whose various garments resemble the ends of the wings of Garuda, who is adorned with various blazing ornaments, and who has her left foot hanging down.
The meditation on Kālī:
[One should meditate upon] Śyāmā, whose eyes are terrifyingly red, whose arms possess the flames of fire,
and who holds with two hands a trident containing a Vetāla together with a *ḍamaruka* drum, and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) in her left hand.
Another [form] holds a bell, a sword, and a pestle; possessing a fierce nature, with three eyes, this is the form of Cāmuṇḍā. Homage to you, Bhuvana-vaśīkaraṇī Bhadrakālī!
[She who dwells] in the house of mercury (rasa), which is the earth-element of the door.
The sixteen [parts] of the foot, nine, and the new nine-fold space;
in the center, a ninefold altar of rice, three spaces in the middle, and five for the sacrificial pit— this is the procedure for the Śiva-maṇḍapa according to the Mānasāra.
The width of the Jyeṣṭha-maṇḍapa is said to be two or three cubits;
it should be provided with eight pillars and [constructed] according to the kalās.
One should construct a four-pillared pavilion in the center of that [area];
within the middle pavilion, one should place the Tārā with two rows of hands.
It is joined with thirty-six pillars and is well-determined according to the *dharmatāla* measure.
As before, one should leave out [the previous area] and in the center, there should be a very extensive space of twelve cubits (*ravihasta*),
joined with sixteen pillars and having a height of eight *tāla* measures.
The pavilion should be known as threefold: small, medium, and large.
For the installation of small lingas, the pavilion should be of the small size.
For the three types of lingas, the pavilion (maṇḍapa) should be of medium size;
it may be either a hut (kuṭa) or a hall (pravā), and the pavilion should be well-decorated.
Or else, there may be eighty-one squares starting from the center;
in its middle, there is a nine-square altar, sixteen [squares] for the main altar, and [one] for the sub-altar.
The height [of the mirror] should be one cubit;
it should be well-remembered as eight finger-breadths in thickness.
It is provided with four side-altars and furnished with a central pillar.
In the middle of the lineage, there is one foot; Brahma has eight,
while Devika has sixteen, Paiśāca twenty-four, and Mānuṣa [twenty-eight].
The thirty-two-fold station is the protection; the eighty-fold station is the Guru.
Within the thousand-fold station of Śiva and Śakti, Brahmā is the Lord of Gods among the eight Vidyeśvaras.
If [one offers] sacrificial pits made of silver and so forth, and garments... (P. 14a, bl.ked) (P.
14b, 1st line) [The meditation on Somāskanda:
One-faced, with four arms, three-eyed, white and radiant, adorned with all ornaments.
I bow to the auspicious Lord who holds in his hands a bracelet with the luster of coral, a *bhṛṅgin* staff, and a *ṭaṅka* axe;
who carries a vessel in his left hand and a sea-monster (*makara*) at his right ear; whose matted hair is adorned with a crown and the moon;
whose garment hangs down, and whose feet rest upon the moon and Guha.
Kṛṣṇa, whose left foot is extended and resting upon a deer, grants the gestures of fearlessness and boons;
he is joined by [the goddess] who, with her left hand, holds a chisel and a bracelet.
One should worship the Lord of Umā and Guha, accompanied by the Goddess whose two feet are joined at the waist while hanging down in sleep, and joined by Skanda, who holds two lotuses in his hands.

Resembling a *drumana* tree with a single face and four arms, holding a black antelope, an axe, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, he possesses three eyes and is clothed in garments.
The meditation on the single-footed form [of Gaṇeśa], who bears the moon upon his head, and whose sons are Gaurī and Hara.
Three-eyed and single-faced, with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness,
standing upright on one leg, seated upon a white lotus throne—
this is the meditation on Trimūrti.
With a red face and three eyes, his hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
joined with a black axe, he is adorned with a crown of matted locks. He stands upright, supported by one leg while the other is slightly bent.
Above the region of the hips, however, are Brahmā and Viṣṇu, joined in a pair;

their hands are placed in the *añjali* gesture, while their other hands display the boon-granting (*vara*) mudrā as before. He is the triple-formed (*trimūrti*), with one arm, three eyes, and one face.
His two shoulders were adorned with the design of sea-monsters, his head was decorated with a crown of matted hair,
and he held a conch and a discus in his two raised left hands.
She is described as having two lotus feet with joined soles and three heads.
She is seated comfortably in the *sukhāsana* posture, sitting at ease upon her seat while holding a bee and an axe.
The right hand displays the gesture of fearlessness, and the left hand displays the gesture of granting boons.
One should avoid the Kaṭaka and Sukhāsīna postures, as well as Umāskanda.
[The meditation on] Dakṣiṇāmūrtti is characterized by a serene countenance and a hand adorned with the gestures (mudrā), a book, fire, a serpent, and a noose.

For the attainment of one's desired goals, one should meditate upon the Lord of Bhavānī— the teacher of the gods who dwells within the Nyagrodha tree, the primordial source of the meaning of the Vedas, the dispeller of ignorance, resplendent with a crown shining like a digit of the moon and adorned with ornaments of pearl necklaces.
With a body pure and white, wearing a serpent as his sacred thread,
his hand joined with fire, and his end adorned by a rosary of beads.
I praise Dakṣiṇāmūrti, who has quivering golden locks and arched brows and eyes,
and who rests upon the cool peak of the best of mountains.
The meditation on the emergence of the *liṅga*:
From the upper part of the *liṅga*-form, Brahmā arose; having assumed the form of a swan (*haṃsa*), and Viṣṇu likewise fashioned himself into the form of a boar (*varāha*) from the *liṅga*.
Brahmā and Viṣṇu, joined with palms pressed together, should be placed at the two sides;
in the middle of the liṅga, however, Candraśekhara should be fashioned as before.
The meditation on Gaurī:
[She is] dark-complexioned, two-eyed, two-armed, and in the *tribhaṅga* posture;
her right and left feet are placed with the toes curled inward.
With a blue lotus in her right hand and a bracelet in her left, the Supreme Goddess rests her hand [upon him].
She has two eyes and two arms; she is dark-complexioned, yet she makes Gaurī fair.
She is adorned with a crown-jewel box and decorated with all ornaments;
she may wear a diadem-crown, or her hair may be tied up,
or she may be endowed with all auspicious marks and have a long garland hanging from her left side.
The goddess is endowed with two arms, one of which is extended; she holds a blue lotus in her left hand, is adorned with all ornaments,
wears a crown shaped like a casket, and is possessed of two eyes.
He was seated, possessed of a dark complexion, like a spider on its web.
The wise practitioner should meditate upon the supreme Gaurī in her bound form,
clothed in silken garments and adorned with all ornaments.
With all her limbs complete and endowed with all the auspicious marks,
she has a bracelet on her right arm and a water-jar hanging from her left hand.
There, by the power of Abhaya, one should carefully smear the thread;
likewise, the wise practitioner should visualize it in the form of Gaurī.
The hundredth part of a śambhu is called a samabhaṅga;
therein, the three faces and the primordial nature are well-adorned.
With a right ear adorned by a hanging blue lotus and a face whose essence is a mind characterized by modesty,
one should meditate upon Sadāśiva,
who resembles pure crystal and is endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man.
Seated in the lotus posture, five-faced, with three eyes in each face.
The face of Tatpuruṣa is yellow, with large eyes, endowed with the digit of the moon of knowledge,
and possesses a white [upper] face;
it is joined with the black face of Aghora and the face of Ugra which has a red luster.
The one facing west, which is very white, is proclaimed as Sadyojāta.
He wore a sacred thread of serpents, was peaceful, adorned with matted locks and a crescent moon,
his limbs anointed with divine perfumes and decorated with celestial flowers.
With his excellent and active hands, he holds a spear, a trident, and a khaṭvāṅga in his right hands,
while with his left hands he bears a ḍamaru drum,
a citron fruit, a serpent, a rosary, and a blue lotus— thus carrying these with five hands.
Resembling jasmine, snow, and crystal, adorned with a crown of matted locks,
endowed with five heads and possessed of five faces.
The face, in particular, is endowed with three eyes;
he has ten arms, a single body, and two feet, and is seated upon a lotus.
In his right hands, he holds a trident, an axe, a sword, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
In his left [hands], he holds a serpent, a noose, a goad, a bell, and fire;
endowed with all ornaments and adorned with every jewel,
the god wears celestial garments, has long arms, and three eyes.
With limbs anointed with divine perfumes and adorned with celestial garlands,
this form should be peaceful, with a face slightly smiling.
One should constantly meditate upon this form, which grants the accomplishment of dharma, kāma, and artha;
it is the visualization of the manifest Sadāśiva,
whose face reaches to the crest of his matted locks and who is adorned with the crescent moon as a head-ornament.
The body, joined with five [elements] and joined with two feet.
One should fashion its eastern face as bright, with cheeks and lips reddened,
and its two arms resembling refined gold.
In his right hand he holds a rosary, and in his left a bījapūraka fruit;
his right side resembles collyrium, and his face is turned toward the moon.
With matted hair bound by a serpent and joined at the temples,
possessing a prominent beard on the tip of his head, he held a trident and a bell in his two hands.
The northern face on the left, however, has the luster of a pomegranate flower;
it is adorned with ornaments, wide-eyed, and endowed with a gaping mouth.
He was endowed with hands holding an axe and a blue lotus, possessed a reddish luster in the west,
was invested in the attire of a youth, and had the face of a white lotus.
The fifth [face], resembling crystal, is exceedingly peaceful and slightly smiling; it possesses the gesture of granting fearlessness (*abhayamudrā*) and is adorned with all ornaments.
From the upper face of Īśāna, the two hands are adorned with bracelets.
It is empowered, joined with a face, and anointed with the colors of a face.
In the Kali age, he is rich in form, adorned with all ornaments,
the granter of all desires, peaceful, and endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man.
One should fashion the body and limbs of Īśāna facing the door,
in accordance with the respective rites, for the sake of attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
One should fashion the shape, the colors, the divine weapons, and the very gateways; one should also construct the body of Īśāna exactly as described in the Darśatāla.

The bodies [of the deities] have the Puruṣa as their foremost [manifestation], existing solely for the sake of the body of the Lord. One should meditate upon the Supreme Power (Parāśakti), who has four arms, three eyes, and a single face, and who is exceedingly gracious.
The goddess, clad in a bud-like garment and adorned with a basket-shaped crown.
She is endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, holding a noose and a goad in her hands;
alternatively, she may hold a blue lotus, or she may hold a trident and a noose.
She wields at will various missiles, holds a conch and a discus in her hands, possesses six arms,
has a face made terrifying by fangs, five faces, and ten arms.
Whether she is seated on a throne as commanded by the god, intent on embracing the god,
standing upon the god's lap, or joined with him in a standing posture;
With her left leg extended, or with her left sandal hanging down.
(P.20a, bl.ked)(P.20b, a1st line) (Side heading: Meditation on the twenty-five forms)
The first [form] holds the moon; the second is accompanied by Umā;
the third is mounted upon a bull; the fourth is in the form of a dance.
One should know the fifth to be the external [practice], and likewise the sixth is the wandering for alms;
one should know Kāmārī as the seventh, and Kālahā would be the eighth.
The ninth is Tripurāri, the thirteenth is Jalandhara,
the eleventh is Gajarī, and the twelfth is Vīrabhadra.
The thirteenth is the form of Hari; the fourteenth is Ardhanārī;
the fifteenth would be Kirāta; and the sixteenth would be Kaṅkāla.
Then the "Grace of Caṇḍeśa" shall be the seventeenth,
and the "Removal of Poison" is recorded as the eighteenth.
The nature of the gift of the discus (cakradāna) is said to consist of nineteen [chapters];
the twentieth is the propitiation of obstacles (vighnaprasāda), and after that follows the Soma-skanda [chapter].
Twenty-two [finger-breadths] shall be for the one-legged [posture], twenty-three for the *sukhāsana*;
the form of Dakṣiṇāmūrti is proclaimed to be twenty-four [finger-breadths].
The nature of the Liṅgodbhava consists of twenty-five varieties;
these are proclaimed as the different forms and manifestations of Maheśvara.
The meditation on Candraśekhara:
[He has] a broad face and eyes, with a gentle and amorous expression;
his hands display the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons, and he bears the crescent moon upon his crest.
He stood in a posture with straight, even feet, resembling coral in hue,
holding a deer and an axe, and seated upon a lotus pedestal.
The god stands in a posture of straightness, joined with a black axe,
his hands granting boons and fearlessness, and adorned with a crown of matted locks.
One should meditate upon the form of the moon-crested Lord, gentle and smiling with a gracious glance, wearing divine garments of skin, together with Umā.
The meditation on the one embraced by Candraśekhara:
(omitting the intervening portion) Gaurī alone, joined with [the Lord] born from her own source, is united with Gaurī;
the Goddess embraces the God with one hand while He stands before her.
The *kṛtā* embrace has been described; thus, it is said to be threefold. Furthermore, there are the *kevala*, the *samapāda*, and likewise the *sahaja* standing postures (*sthānaka*).
Having embraced the moon-crested Lord, who possesses the [three] folds [of skin],
one should meditate upon Him together with Umā— He who is white-hued, seated on a comfortable throne, and joined by the Goddess.
The Hariṇī mudrā, which bestows the boons of the deer-horn and fearlessness.
This is the very form of Lord Śiva together with Umā, holding a blue lotus, bestowing boons, and possessing a gracious countenance.
The meditation on the vertical *tāṇḍava*:
situated in the *apasmāra* [stance] during the dialogue with Kālī’s vow,
the right foot is bent and held by the head of the left foot.
With a smiling face and three eyes, possessing twelve arms and twelve eyes,
wearing a tiger-skin garment and his body smeared with ashes.
Tawny-hued and endowed with matted locks, adorned with the wings of a crane,
difficult to restrain, bearing the arka flower, and accompanied by the crescent moon.
With his left hand raised above his head, he hangs from the right hip;
in his right hands, he holds a trident, an arrow, a mace, a sword, and a bell.
In her left hands, she holds a skull-bowl, a noose, a ḍamaru drum, a cow, and a serpent;
she is described as having upward-pointing hair and is accompanied by Kālī and Lañjā.
He has one face and three eyes, is adorned with a crown of matted locks,
and stands with his right foot slightly bent, treading upon an epileptic spirit.
The left foot should be raised above the head, and the left hand placed upon the head;
[the other hands hold] the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), a trident, a hand-drum (ḍamaru), and a śālaja musical instrument.
Adorned with eight arms bearing a serpent, fire, and a girdle,
he is engaged in the meditation of wandering for alms;
he possesses a skull as his form of fire and is equipped with a trident in his hand.
The hand-drum is joined with a deer-mouth for the purpose of offering grass.
Endowed with all auspicious marks, adorned with all kinds of ashes,
equipped with sandals, and surrounded by all beings.
The Great Lord (Maheśvara) wandering for alms is joined with Kuṇḍodara;
Kāmārī is of fierce form, meditated upon as being endowed with four arms.
Accompanied by a black *aṭaṅka* [seal], and endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness (*abhaya*) and bestowing boons (*varada*).
Thus, for one desiring success, I shall describe the destroyer of Time (Kāla):
the three-eyed Lord, intent on beholding the Goddess, seated upon a radiant throne,
with hands bearing the mudrā and the ṭaṅka, arms reaching down to his knees, and a gracious countenance.
I bow to Hara, the enemy of Smara, who observes the vow of a sage with a serpent bound around his waist,
whose body is smeared with ashes, who bears the moon, and who is adorned with matted locks and a braided tuft.
One should meditate upon the Lord of Yoga himself, seated in the heroic posture (vīrāsana), holding a pure black antelope skin,
with his palm placed upon his left thigh.
One should worship the Lord of Smara (Kāmeśvara), who is the enemy of Kāma, the roar of a tiger, and whose forehead is adorned with a third eye;
he is the meditation on the destruction of Time (Kāla),
possessing four arms or three eyes, and especially two arms.
In the right hand there is a trident, while in the left it is known as a needle on the fingers.
One should especially meditate on the Lord who grants fearlessness and boons, whose hand rests upon his thigh,
and who destroys Time by treading with his left foot.

three-eyed and single-faced, adorned with the crescent moon upon his matted locks;

has one foot tucked up on the left side, while the other stands upon a wooden sandal.

I worship the one who wears a tiger-skin garment, whose feet are adorned with two rows of tinkling anklets, and who bears a crown;
may I meditate upon him.
The meditation on the Kaṅkāla form:
his feet are joined with sandals, he is endowed with four arms,
wears a sacred thread, is perfectly tranquil, has a beautiful face, and is most resplendent.
Adorned with a crown of a half-moon,
his right foot is slightly bent and his left foot is firmly planted, well-positioned upon the lap of his father-in-law.
Or else, one whose own limbs possess symmetry and luster should hold a *paraśu* (axe) in the right hand,

I bow down to the Sun, who resembles a hibiscus flower, the son of Kaśyapa, of great splendor,

I bow down to the auspicious Kumāra, born from the womb of the earth, resembling lightning and gold, with a spear in his hand.

I bow to that Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods and the sages, who resembles gold, who is worthy of worship, and the lord of the three worlds.
I bow down to Bhārgava, the descendant of Bhrigu, who possesses golden jars, who is equal to Śiva, the supreme preceptor of the Daityas, and the expounder of all scriptures.
